blocks.x: Key definitions

AutoFormat A built-in collection of preset table formats (fonts, borders, shading, number formats) that can be applied to a selected range in one click via Home > Format as Table, previewed by hovering over a style before selecting it.

Format Painter A toolbar tool that copies all formatting from one cell (or range) and applies it elsewhere. A single click copies to one destination; double-clicking the Format Painter button keeps it “on” so the format can be pasted onto multiple, non-adjacent destinations; press Esc to turn it off.
Point (font size) The unit fonts are measured in. 1 inch = 72 points. A 12-point font is therefore roughly 1/6 of an inch tall.
Concatenation Joining text and/or numbers from different cells into one string using the & operator, e.g. =B12&TEXT(C12,"####") can produce “Final Sales for1999”.

Currency vs. Accounting Both display a currency symbol, but Currency places the symbol immediately next to the number, while Accounting format aligns the currency symbols and the decimal points in a column, giving the tidy, ledger-style look used in financial statements.

Presentation tools
From one-click table styles and format copying to character-level styling, fonts, merging, wrapping and joining text with the concatenation operator.
AutoFormat — Format as Table

Excel ships with a gallery of preset table formats — ready-made combinations of borders, shading, font weight and number formatting. To use one: select the data range, open Home > Format as Table (in the Style group of the ribbon), and hover over a thumbnail to preview it live on the worksheet before clicking to apply it. This is the fastest way to make a plain table of figures look professional without manually setting borders and shading cell by cell.
The Format Painter

Format Painter workflow 1. Select the cell (or range) whose formatting you want to copy. 2. Click the Format Painter button (the paintbrush icon on the Home tab). 3. Click (or drag across) the destination cell(s) — the formatting is pasted, and the tool switches itself off. To copy the same format to several separate, non-adjacent destinations, double-click the Format Painter button instead of single-clicking. It then stays active so you can click multiple destinations in turn; press Esc (or click the button again) when finished to release it.
Formatting selected characters within a cell

Excel formatting isn't limited to whole cells. Click into the cell to edit mode (or select the cell and work in the formula bar), then drag to highlight only the characters you want to change within that cell's text. With those characters selected, apply Bold, Italic, Underline, or open the Format Cells dialog (Font tab) for finer control — e.g. making only the word “TOTAL” bold inside a longer cell label, while the rest of the text stays plain.
Formatting shortcut keys

c: Toggles bold on the selected cell(s)/characters
Toggles a line through the text

blocks.x: Fonts & font styles

items: ptFont size is measured in points, where 1 inch = 72 points. Larger point values give taller, larger characters.
AbThe four basic font styles available are plain (regular), bold, italic and underline — and these can be combined, e.g. bold italic.
SStrikethrough is also a supported style, useful for marking items as completed, removed, or superseded without deleting them.
256A single worksheet can use up to 256 different fonts, though good design practice keeps a workbook to just one or two font families for consistency.

blocks.x: Centering, merging & wrapping text

Merge and Center The Merge and Center button (Home tab, Alignment group) combines the selected cells into one single cell and horizontally centers its content — the classic way to center a worksheet title across several columns.

Merge Across (Selection) Available from Format Cells > Alignment tab > Horizontal dropdown > Center Across Selection (or the Merge Across command), this centers text visually across the selected cells without actually merging them into one cell — each underlying cell keeps its own identity, unlike Merge and Center.

Wrap Text Turns on with the Wrap Text button (Home > Alignment group) or via Format Cells > Alignment tab > Wrap Text checkbox. It makes long text wrap onto multiple lines within the same cell, automatically increasing the row height to fit — instead of the text overflowing into (or being cut off by) neighbouring cells.

Merge Cells In the same Alignment tab of Format Cells, ticking the Merge Cells checkbox combines the selected range into a single cell (content is kept only from the top-left cell of the original selection).
Concatenation with the & operator

The ampersand & joins (concatenates) text strings, cell references and function results into one combined text value. It is commonly paired with TEXT() to control how a number is displayed inside the joined string.

Worked concatenation example =B12&TEXT(C12,"####") If cell B12 contains the text “Final Sales for” and cell C12 contains the number 1999, this formula produces the single text string “Final Sales for1999”. Note there is no automatic space — if one is wanted, it must be added explicitly, e.g. =B12&" "&TEXT(C12,"####").
Displaying values
How Excel auto-detects number formats as you type, the three ways to apply a format, the shortcut keys, and the full set of built-in format categories.
Excel's automatic number formatting
Excel often detects the kind of number you're typing and applies a matching format automatically:

items: $Typing $12.95 into a cell automatically applies Currency format, showing the dollar sign and two decimal places.

%Typing 15% displays as 15% on the worksheet, but the underlying stored value is 0.15 — that is what appears in the formula bar when the cell is selected. Percentage format simply multiplies the stored value by 100 and appends the % sign for display.

blocks.x: Displayed value vs. stored value What you see in the cell is the formatted display; what Excel actually stores and calculates with is the raw number, visible by selecting the cell and reading the formula bar. This distinction matters for percentages in particular.
Applying a number format

items: 1Toolbar/ribbon: use the Number Format dropdown (Home tab, Number group) to pick General, Number, Currency, Percentage, etc. directly, or the small currency/percent/comma icon buttons beside it.
2Menu/dialog: Home > Format Cells > Number tab (or right-click > Format Cells) gives full control — category, decimal places, symbol, negative-number style, etc.
3Keyboard shortcuts: the five Ctrl+Shift shortcuts below apply a format instantly without opening any menu.

blocks.x: Number format shortcut keys

c: Two decimal places with thousands separator, e.g. 1,234.00
Currency symbol, 2 decimal places, parentheses for negatives
Value ×100 with a % sign, no decimal places

blocks.x: Built-in number format categories

c: Excel's default; no specific number format. Automatically switches to scientific notation for very large numbers (about 12+ digits).
General display of numbers with control over decimal places, thousands separator, and how negatives are shown.
Used for general monetary values; adds the default currency symbol and 2 decimals. Symbol sits directly against the digits.
Aligns currency symbols and decimal points in a column, giving neat, ledger-style columns of figures — this alignment is what distinguishes it from Currency.
Displays date/time serial values as calendar dates or clock times. Formats marked with an asterisk (*) respond automatically to date/time settings in Windows Control Panel (regional settings).
Multiplies the cell value by 100 and displays a % sign; the stored value stays the original decimal.
Displays a decimal value as a fraction, with a chosen denominator precision.
Useful for tracking list and database values such as ZIP codes, phone numbers and Social Security numbers.
Displays a number in exponential notation, replacing part of the number with E+n.
Cell content is treated as text, even if it looks like a number, and is displayed exactly as typed (left-aligned).
Allows creation of a personal number-format code by editing an existing format; Excel permits between 200 and 250 custom formats per workbook, depending on the language version installed.

blocks.title: Currency vs. Accounting — the key distinction

blocks.x: Both formats add a currency symbol and two decimal places by default, and both are frequently confused. The difference to remember for the exam:

items: Currency format places the currency symbol immediately to the left of the digits of each number, so symbols line up only if the digit counts happen to match.

Accounting format fixes the currency symbol at the left edge of the cell and right-aligns the decimal points, so a whole column of figures lines up neatly under one another — the standard look for financial statements and ledgers.

blocks.x: Worksheet layout
Three ways to resize a column so its content fits, and two ways to hide or unhide columns.
Adjusting column width

items: 1Mouse-drag: position the pointer on the border between two column headers (it becomes a double-headed arrow) and drag left or right to the desired width.
2Double-click to AutoFit: double-click that same column-header border to instantly resize the column to fit the width of its widest entry.
3Menu method: Home > Format (Cells group) offers Column Width (type an exact value), AutoFit Column Width, and Default Width (resets to the workbook's standard column width).

blocks.x: Select column(s)→ Drag border, or→ Home > Format > Column Width→ Column resized
Hiding & unhiding columns

Method 1 — drag the column separator Drag the right-hand border of a column header all the way to the left, past the left border, to collapse the column's width to zero and hide it. To unhide, position the pointer precisely on the thin double line marking the hidden column, then drag it back out.

Method 2 — the Format menu Select the column(s), then go to Home > Format > Hide & Unhide > Hide Columns (or select a range spanning the hidden column and choose Unhide Columns). This menu route is more reliable than dragging because it doesn't depend on pinpointing a near-invisible border with the mouse.

items: Hiding keeps the underlying data and formulas intact — formulas that reference a hidden column still calculate correctly.
It's commonly used to conceal helper columns (intermediate calculations) or sensitive data (e.g. cost columns) before printing or sharing a worksheet.
A hidden column can always be restored via Unhide; a deleted column's data is gone unless undone immediately.

sections.title: Formatting propagates to every grouped sheet

blocks.x: Multi-sheet efficiency
Apply one formatting action to several worksheets simultaneously by grouping their tabs.

Grouping worksheets Click a sheet tab, then hold Shift and click another tab to select every tab between them (adjacent group), or hold Ctrl and click individual tabs one at a time to select non-adjacent sheets. All selected tabs highlight, and the workbook's title bar shows [Group] next to the file name.
Formatting propagates to every grouped sheet

Once sheets are grouped, any formatting command you apply — fonts, borders, number formats, column widths, cell merges, even typed entries — is performed on the active sheet (the one currently in front) and is automatically applied to every other sheet in the group, in the same cell positions. This is a fast way to make several monthly or regional worksheets that share the same layout look identical without repeating the work sheet by sheet.
Shift-click or Ctrl-click tabs→ Title bar shows [Group]→ Format the active sheet→ Change applies to all grouped sheets
Ungrouping sheets

Ungroup Click any single sheet tab (one that is not being multi-selected) to break the group — the [Group] indicator disappears from the title bar, and formatting commands from that point on affect only the active sheet again. Right-clicking a grouped tab and choosing Ungroup Sheets works too.

blocks.title: Practical cautions when working with grouped sheets

items: Because typed entries also propagate while sheets are grouped, it's easy to accidentally overwrite data on other sheets — always check the title bar for [Group] before typing.
Remember to ungroup as soon as the shared formatting is done, so later edits don't unintentionally spread to every sheet.
Grouping is ideal for identically laid-out worksheets (e.g. Jan, Feb, Mar tabs with the same headings) but can create confusing results on sheets with different layouts.
